title: The Economics of Attention
author: David Didau
summary: Didau extends his earlier ecological metaphor for school improvement -- schools as systems with a 'carrying capacity' -- into an economic framing, arguing that attention, not money or time, is the truly scarce resource school leaders manage. He contrasts the rigorous procurement scrutiny applied to a £100,000 IT system with the near-total absence of accounting for a new book-scrutiny initiative, even though the latter can consume thousands of cumulative staff hours across planning, INSET delivery, departmental discussion, and follow-up. Drawing on research into task-switching costs (Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans) and 'attention residue' (Sophie Leroy), he explains why simply protecting teachers' time with non-contact periods does not reliably protect their attention, since fragmented, interrupted time produces the same tunnelling and cognitive cost as genuine scarcity. He borrows Ronald Coase's concept of transaction costs to argue that every new school initiative imposes ongoing coordination costs paid in attention, not just an initial rollout cost, and proposes an 'attentional return on investment' framework asking whether routines are replacing reminders and expertise is replacing compliance over time. His central leadership claim is that protecting staff attention is as much a leadership responsibility as creating time, and that schools which fail to calculate attentional costs risk accumulating 'attentional debt' from initiatives that never pay off. This is category Education - Practice & Culture rather than Ed-Tech because the piece is about school-leadership attention economics generally, not AI or technology as its subject.
points: Didau contrasts the rigorous procurement scrutiny schools apply to a £100,000 IT purchase with the near-total absence of cost-accounting for a new book-scrutiny initiative, even though the latter can consume thousands of cumulative staff hours.

Citing Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans, he notes that task-switching carries a reliable cognitive penalty, and that knowledge workers took an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to return to an interrupted task -- meaning non-contact time on a timetable does not guarantee genuine attentional capacity.
Sophie Leroy's concept of 'attention residue' explains why unfinished tasks continue occupying part of a person's thinking even after they've physically moved to something else.

Applying Ronald Coase's concept of transaction costs to schools, Didau argues that every new initiative imposes ongoing coordination costs, paid in attention, that are easy to overlook because they arrive in small, unnoticed instalments.

His proposed diagnostic for any school initiative: is it becoming easier to sustain, are routines replacing reminders, and is expertise replacing compliance -- if not, the school may be accumulating attentional debt without generating attentional returns.
quotes: Quite rightly, schools are meticulous about accounting for money, with every significant expenditure needing to be justified. Do time and attention deserve the same discipline?

According to William Ocasio, organisations become what their members collectively pay attention to. In schools, what leaders look for occupies teachers' minds, just as what teachers look for occupies students' minds.

Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans found that switching between tasks carries a reliable cognitive penalty. Each time we switch between tasks we not only lose time, we also increase the likelihood of mistakes.
Research has found that, after an interruption, knowledge workers took an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to return to their original task, often after completing several other tasks first.

This narrowing of attention results in an effect they call tunnelling: when a resource becomes scarce, immediate demands dominate our thinking, making it harder to focus on longer-term, more strategic concerns.
Creating more time certainly helps, but it won't result in more attentional capacity. Creating time is a scheduling challenge whereas as protecting attention is organisational design challenge.
If the answer's no, you may be accumulating attentional debt without generating attentional returns.
